# Siṅghapupphajātaka (Ja 392)
**ID:** Ja 392
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Siṅghapupphajātaka
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja392
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul5.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Siṅghapupphajātaka* (also titled *Bhisapupphajātaka*) is a birth story belonging to the Jātaka collection of the Pali Canon [SuttaCentral; Ānandajoti 2010]. In the framing narrative (*paccuppannavatthu*), the Buddha is residing at Jetavana when he delivers the discourse concerning a monk who had gone to dwell in a forest in the Kosala country [SuttaCentral]. After the monk waded into a lotus pool and smelled a blooming lotus flower, an indwelling forest goddess rebuked him as a "thief of odours" [SuttaCentral; Ānandajoti 2010]. When the monk questioned why she reprimanded him for smelling a blossom rather than rebuking a person who cut down the lotuses, she noted that to the pure of heart even a minute flaw seems great [Ānandajoti 2010]. Returning frightened to Jetavana, the monk recounted the incident to the Buddha, who explained that sages of the past had likewise been challenged by a deity when smelling a flower and related the tale of the past [SuttaCentral].
Curated parallels on SuttaCentral identify the story's verse and thematic counterpart in the *Saṁyutta Nikāya* (*Gandhatthenasutta*, SN 9.14 in the *Vana Saṁyutta*), as well as in the Chinese *Saṁyuktāgama* traditions (SA 1338 and SA2 358) [SuttaCentral]. Passage-level parallels are also listed with the *Theragāthā* (Thag 14.1 and Thag 17.2) [SuttaCentral]. Text-reuse algorithms in DharmaNexus confirm substantial shared textual material across SN 9 (specifically §0.4–7.4 aligned with SN 9.14), the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā*, the *Theragāthā-aṭṭhakathā*, and cross-language alignments with Chinese translations in the Taishō Canon (T99 and T100) [DharmaNexus].
